       3. [Queue an element task](#8172-queuing-tasks) on the [DOM manipulation task source](#8174-generic-task-sources) given the [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element and finishUpdate.

##### 4.8.4.4 Requirements for providing text to act as an alternative for images

###### 4.8.4.4.1 General guidelines

Except where otherwise specified, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be specified and its value must not be empty; the value must be an appropriate replacement for the image. The specific requirements for the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute depend on what the image is intended to represent, as described in the following sections.

The most general rule to consider when writing alternative text is the following: **the intent is that replacing every image with the text of its [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute does not change the meaning of the page**.

So, in general, alternative text can be written by considering what one would have written had one not been able to include the image.

A corollary to this is that the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute's value should never contain text that could be considered the image's *caption*, *title*, or *legend*. It is supposed to contain replacement text that could be used by users *instead* of the image; it is not meant to supplement the image. The [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute can be used for supplemental information.

Another corollary is that the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute's value should not repeat information that is already provided in the prose next to the image.

> [!note]
> One way to think of alternative text is to think about how you would read the page containing the image to someone over the phone, without mentioning that there is an image present. Whatever you say instead of the image is typically a good start for writing the alternative text.

###### 4.8.4.4.2 A link or button containing nothing but the image

When an [`a`](#451-the-a-element) element that creates a [hyperlink](#461-introduction), or a [`button`](#4106-the-button-element) element, has no textual content but contains one or more images, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attributes must contain text that together convey the purpose of the link or button.

> [!example]
> In this example, a user is asked to pick their preferred color from a list of three. Each color is given by an image, but for users who have configured their user agent not to display images, the color names are used instead:
> 
> ```html
> <h1>Pick your color</h1>
> <ul>
>  <li><a href="green.html"><img src="green.jpeg" alt="Green"></a></li>
>  <li><a href="blue.html"><img src="blue.jpeg" alt="Blue"></a></li>
>  <li><a href="red.html"><img src="red.jpeg" alt="Red"></a></li>
> </ul>
> ```

> [!example]
> In this example, each button has a set of images to indicate the kind of color output desired by the user. The first image is used in each case to give the alternative text.
> 
> ```html
> <button name="rgb"><img src="red" alt="RGB"><img src="green" alt=""><img src="blue" alt=""></button>
> <button name="cmyk"><img src="cyan" alt="CMYK"><img src="magenta" alt=""><img src="yellow" alt=""><img src="black" alt=""></button>
> ```
> 
> Since each image represents one part of the text, it could also be written like this:
> 
> ```html
> <button name="rgb"><img src="red" alt="R"><img src="green" alt="G"><img src="blue" alt="B"></button>
> <button name="cmyk"><img src="cyan" alt="C"><img src="magenta" alt="M"><img src="yellow" alt="Y"><img src="black" alt="K"></button>
> ```
> 
> However, with other alternative text, this might not work, and putting all the alternative text into one image in each case might make more sense:
> 
> ```html
> <button name="rgb"><img src="red" alt="sRGB profile"><img src="green" alt=""><img src="blue" alt=""></button>
> <button name="cmyk"><img src="cyan" alt="CMYK profile"><img src="magenta" alt=""><img src="yellow" alt=""><img src="black" alt=""></button>
> ```

###### 4.8.4.4.3 A phrase or paragraph with an alternative graphical representation: charts, diagrams, graphs, maps, illustrations

Sometimes something can be more clearly stated in graphical form, for example as a flowchart, a diagram, a graph, or a simple map showing directions. In such cases, an image can be given using the [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element, but the lesser textual version must still be given, so that users who are unable to view the image (e.g. because they have a very slow connection, or because they are using a text-only browser, or because they are listening to the page being read out by a hands-free automobile voice web browser, or simply because they are blind) are still able to understand the message being conveyed.

The text must be given in the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute, and must convey the same message as the image specified in the [`src`](#483-the-img-element) attribute.

It is important to realize that the alternative text is a *replacement* for the image, not a description of the image.

> [!example]
> In the following example we have [a flowchart](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/images/parsing-model-overview.svg) in image form, with text in the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute rephrasing the flowchart in prose form:
> 
> ```html
> <p>In the common case, the data handled by the tokenization stage
> comes from the network, but it can also come from script.</p>
> <p><img src="images/parsing-model-overview.svg" alt="The Network
> passes data to the Input Stream Preprocessor, which passes it to the
> Tokenizer, which passes it to the Tree Construction stage. From there,
> data goes to both the DOM and to Script Execution. Script Execution is
> linked to the DOM, and, using document.write(), passes data to the
> Tokenizer."></p>
> ```

> [!example]
> Here's another example, showing a good solution and a bad solution to the problem of including an image in a description.
> 
> First, here's the good solution. This sample shows how the alternative text should just be what you would have put in the prose if the image had never existed.
> 
> ```html
> <!-- This is the correct way to do things. -->
> <p>
>  You are standing in an open field west of a house.
>  <img src="house.jpeg" alt="The house is white, with a boarded front door.">
>  There is a small mailbox here.
> </p>
> ```
> 
> Second, here's the bad solution. In this incorrect way of doing things, the alternative text is simply a description of the image, instead of a textual replacement for the image. It's bad because when the image isn't shown, the text doesn't flow as well as in the first example.
> 
> ```html
> <!-- This is the wrong way to do things. -->
> <p>
>  You are standing in an open field west of a house.
>  <img src="house.jpeg" alt="A white house, with a boarded front door.">
>  There is a small mailbox here.
> </p>
> ```
> 
> Text such as "Photo of white house with boarded door" would be equally bad alternative text (though it could be suitable for the [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute or in the [`figcaption`](#4413-the-figcaption-element) element of a [`figure`](#4412-the-figure-element) with this image).

###### 4.8.4.4.4 A short phrase or label with an alternative graphical representation: icons, logos

A document can contain information in iconic form. The icon is intended to help users of visual browsers to recognize features at a glance.

In some cases, the icon is supplemental to a text label conveying the same meaning. In those cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be present but must be empty.

> [!example]
> Here the icons are next to text that conveys the same meaning, so they have an empty [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute:
> 
> ```html
> <nav>
>  <p><a href="/help/"><img src="/icons/help.png" alt=""> Help</a></p>
>  <p><a href="/configure/"><img src="/icons/configuration.png" alt="">
>  Configuration Tools</a></p>
> </nav>
> ```

In other cases, the icon has no text next to it describing what it means; the icon is supposed to be self-explanatory. In those cases, an equivalent textual label must be given in the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute.

> [!example]
> Here, posts on a news site are labeled with an icon indicating their topic.
> 
> ```html
> <body>
>  <article>
>   <header>
>    <h1>Ratatouille wins <i>Best Movie of the Year</i> award</h1>
>    <p><img src="movies.png" alt="Movies"></p>
>   </header>
>   <p>Pixar has won yet another <i>Best Movie of the Year</i> award,
>   making this its 8th win in the last 12 years.</p>
>  </article>
>  <article>
>   <header>
>    <h1>Latest TWiT episode is online</h1>
>    <p><img src="podcasts.png" alt="Podcasts"></p>
>   </header>
>   <p>The latest TWiT episode has been posted, in which we hear
>   several tech news stories as well as learning much more about the
>   iPhone. This week, the panelists compare how reflective their
>   iPhones' Apple logos are.</p>
>  </article>
> </body>
> ```

Many pages include logos, insignia, flags, or emblems, which stand for a particular entity such as a company, organization, project, band, software package, country, or some such.

If the logo is being used to represent the entity, e.g. as a page heading, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must contain the name of the entity being represented by the logo. The [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must *not* contain text like the word "logo", as it is not the fact that it is a logo that is being conveyed, it's the entity itself.

If the logo is being used next to the name of the entity that it represents, then the logo is supplemental, and its [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must instead be empty.

If the logo is merely used as decorative material (as branding, or, for example, as a side image in an article that mentions the entity to which the logo belongs), then the entry below on purely decorative images applies. If the logo is actually being discussed, then it is being used as a phrase or paragraph (the description of the logo) with an alternative graphical representation (the logo itself), and the first entry above applies.

> [!example]
> In the following snippets, all four of the above cases are present. First, we see a logo used to represent a company:
> 
> ```html
> <h1><img src="XYZ.gif" alt="The XYZ company"></h1>
> ```
> 
> Next, we see a paragraph which uses a logo right next to the company name, and so doesn't have any alternative text:
> 
> ```html
> <article>
>  <h2>News</h2>
>  <p>We have recently been looking at buying the <img src="alpha.gif"
>  alt=""> ΑΒΓ company, a small Greek company
>  specializing in our type of product.</p>
> ```
> 
> In this third snippet, we have a logo being used in an aside, as part of the larger article discussing the acquisition:
> 
> ```html
> <aside><p><img src="alpha-large.gif" alt=""></p></aside>
>  <p>The ΑΒΓ company has had a good quarter, and our
>  pie chart studies of their accounts suggest a much bigger blue slice
>  than its green and orange slices, which is always a good sign.</p>
> </article>
> ```
> 
> Finally, we have an opinion piece talking about a logo, and the logo is therefore described in detail in the alternative text.
> 
> ```html
> <p>Consider for a moment their logo:</p>
> 
> <p><img src="/images/logo" alt="It consists of a green circle with a
> green question mark centered inside it."></p>
> 
> <p>How unoriginal can you get? I mean, oooooh, a question mark, how
> <em>revolutionary</em>, how utterly <em>ground-breaking</em>, I'm
> sure everyone will rush to adopt those specifications now! They could
> at least have tried for some sort of, I don't know, sequence of
> rounded squares with varying shades of green and bold white outlines,
> at least that would look good on the cover of a blue book.</p>
> ```
> 
> This example shows how the alternative text should be written such that if the image isn't *[available](#4843-processing-model)*, and the text is used instead, the text flows seamlessly into the surrounding text, as if the image had never been there in the first place.

###### 4.8.4.4.5 Text that has been rendered to a graphic for typographical effect

Sometimes, an image just consists of text, and the purpose of the image is not to highlight the actual typographic effects used to render the text, but just to convey the text itself.

In such cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be present but must consist of the same text as written in the image itself.

> [!example]
> Consider a graphic containing the text "Earth Day", but with the letters all decorated with flowers and plants. If the text is merely being used as a heading, to spice up the page for graphical users, then the correct alternative text is just the same text "Earth Day", and no mention need be made of the decorations:
> 
> ```html
> <h1><img src="earthdayheading.png" alt="Earth Day"></h1>
> ```

> [!example]
> An illuminated manuscript might use graphics for some of its images. The alternative text in such a situation is just the character that the image represents.
> 
> ```html
> <p><img src="initials/o.svg" alt="O">nce upon a time and a long long time ago, late at
> night, when it was dark, over the hills, through the woods, across a great ocean, in a land far
> away, in a small house, on a hill, under a full moon...
> ```

When an image is used to represent a character that cannot otherwise be represented in Unicode, for example gaiji, itaiji, or new characters such as novel currency symbols, the alternative text should be a more conventional way of writing the same thing, e.g. using the phonetic hiragana or katakana to give the character's pronunciation.

> [!example]
> In this example from 1997, a new-fangled currency symbol that looks like a curly E with two bars in the middle instead of one is represented using an image. The alternative text gives the character's pronunciation.
> 
> ```html
> <p>Only <img src="euro.png" alt="euro ">5.99!
> ```

An image should not be used if characters would serve an identical purpose. Only when the text cannot be directly represented using text, e.g., because of decorations or because there is no appropriate character (as in the case of gaiji), would an image be appropriate.

> [!note]
> If an author is tempted to use an image because their default system font does not support a given character, then web fonts are a better solution than images.

###### 4.8.4.4.6 A graphical representation of some of the surrounding text

In many cases, the image is actually just supplementary, and its presence merely reinforces the surrounding text. In these cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be present but its value must be the empty string.

In general, an image falls into this category if removing the image doesn't make the page any less useful, but including the image makes it a lot easier for users of visual browsers to understand the concept.

> [!example]
> A flowchart that repeats the previous paragraph in graphical form:
> 
> ```html
> <p>The Network passes data to the Input Stream Preprocessor, which
> passes it to the Tokenizer, which passes it to the Tree Construction
> stage. From there, data goes to both the DOM and to Script Execution.
> Script Execution is linked to the DOM, and, using document.write(),
> passes data to the Tokenizer.</p>
> <p><img src="images/parsing-model-overview.svg" alt=""></p>
> ```
> 
> In these cases, it would be wrong to include alternative text that consists of just a caption. If a caption is to be included, then either the [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute can be used, or the [`figure`](#4412-the-figure-element) and [`figcaption`](#4413-the-figcaption-element) elements can be used. In the latter case, the image would in fact be a phrase or paragraph with an alternative graphical representation, and would thus require alternative text.
> 
> ```html
> <!-- Using the title="" attribute -->
> <p>The Network passes data to the Input Stream Preprocessor, which
> passes it to the Tokenizer, which passes it to the Tree Construction
> stage. From there, data goes to both the DOM and to Script Execution.
> Script Execution is linked to the DOM, and, using document.write(),
> passes data to the Tokenizer.</p>
> <p><img src="images/parsing-model-overview.svg" alt=""
>         title="Flowchart representation of the parsing model."></p>
> ```
> 
> ```html
> <!-- Using <figure> and <figcaption> -->
> <p>The Network passes data to the Input Stream Preprocessor, which
> passes it to the Tokenizer, which passes it to the Tree Construction
> stage. From there, data goes to both the DOM and to Script Execution.
> Script Execution is linked to the DOM, and, using document.write(),
> passes data to the Tokenizer.</p>
> <figure>
>  <img src="images/parsing-model-overview.svg" alt="The Network leads to
>  the Input Stream Preprocessor, which leads to the Tokenizer, which
>  leads to the Tree Construction stage. The Tree Construction stage
>  leads to two items. The first is Script Execution, which leads via
>  document.write() back to the Tokenizer. The second item from which
>  Tree Construction leads is the DOM. The DOM is related to the Script
>  Execution.">
>  <figcaption>Flowchart representation of the parsing model.</figcaption>
> </figure>
> ```
> 
> ```html
> <!-- This is WRONG. Do not do this. Instead, do what the above examples do. -->
> <p>The Network passes data to the Input Stream Preprocessor, which
> passes it to the Tokenizer, which passes it to the Tree Construction
> stage. From there, data goes to both the DOM and to Script Execution.
> Script Execution is linked to the DOM, and, using document.write(),
> passes data to the Tokenizer.</p>
> <p><img src="images/parsing-model-overview.svg"
>         alt="Flowchart representation of the parsing model."></p>
> <!-- Never put the image's caption in the alt="" attribute! -->
> ```

> [!example]
> A graph that repeats the previous paragraph in graphical form:
> 
> ```html
> <p>According to a study covering several billion pages,
> about 62% of documents on the web in 2007 triggered the Quirks
> rendering mode of web browsers, about 30% triggered the Almost
> Standards mode, and about 9% triggered the Standards mode.</p>
> <p><img src="rendering-mode-pie-chart.png" alt=""></p>
> ```

###### 4.8.4.4.7 Ancillary images

Sometimes, an image is not critical to the content, but is nonetheless neither purely decorative nor entirely redundant with the text. In these cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be present, and its value should either be the empty string, or a textual representation of the information that the image conveys. If the image has a caption giving the image's title, then the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute's value must not be empty (as that would be quite confusing for non-visual readers).

> [!example]
> Consider a news article about a political figure, in which the individual's face was shown in an image. The image is not purely decorative, as it is relevant to the story. The image is not entirely redundant with the story either, as it shows what the politician looks like. Whether any alternative text need be provided is an authoring decision, decided by whether the image influences the interpretation of the prose.
> 
> In this first variant, the image is shown without context, and no alternative text is provided:
> 
> ```html
> <p><img src="president.jpeg" alt=""> Ahead of today's referendum,
> the President wrote an open letter to all registered voters. In it, she admitted that the country was
> divided.</p>
> ```
> 
> If the picture is just a face, there might be no value in describing it. It's of no interest to the reader whether the individual has red hair or blond hair, whether the individual has white skin or black skin, whether the individual has one eye or two eyes.
> 
> However, if the picture is more dynamic, for instance showing the politician as angry, or particularly happy, or devastated, some alternative text would be useful in setting the tone of the article, a tone that might otherwise be missed:
> 
> ```html
> <p><img src="president.jpeg" alt="The President is sad.">
> Ahead of today's referendum, the President wrote an open letter to all
> registered voters. In it, she admitted that the country was divided.
> </p>
> ```
> 
> ```html
> <p><img src="president.jpeg" alt="The President is happy!">
> Ahead of today's referendum, the President wrote an open letter to all
> registered voters. In it, she admitted that the country was divided.
> </p>
> ```
> 
> Whether the individual was "sad" or "happy" makes a difference to how the rest of the paragraph is to be interpreted: is she likely saying that she is unhappy with the country being divided, or is she saying that the prospect of a divided country is good for her political career? The interpretation varies based on the image.

> [!example]
> If the image has a caption, then including alternative text avoids leaving the non-visual user confused as to what the caption refers to.
> 
> ```html
> <p>Ahead of today's referendum, the President wrote an open letter to
> all registered voters. In it, she admitted that the country was divided.</p>
> <figure>
>  <img src="president.jpeg"
>       alt="A high forehead, cheerful disposition, and dark hair round out the President's face.">
>  <figcaption> The President of Ruritania. Photo © 2014 PolitiPhoto. </figcaption>
> </figure>
> ```

###### 4.8.4.4.8 A purely decorative image that doesn't add any information

If an image is decorative but isn't especially page-specific — for example an image that forms part of a site-wide design scheme — the image should be specified in the site's CSS, not in the markup of the document.

However, a decorative image that isn't discussed by the surrounding text but still has some relevance can be included in a page using the [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element. Such images are decorative, but still form part of the content. In these cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be present but its value must be the empty string.

> [!example]
> Examples where the image is purely decorative despite being relevant would include things like a photo of the Black Rock City landscape in a blog post about an event at Burning Man, or an image of a painting inspired by a poem, on a page reciting that poem. The following snippet shows an example of the latter case (only the first verse is included in this snippet):
> 
> ```html
> <h1>The Lady of Shalott</h1>
> <p><img src="shalott.jpeg" alt=""></p>
> <p>On either side the river lie<br>
> Long fields of barley and of rye,<br>
> That clothe the wold and meet the sky;<br>
> And through the field the road run by<br>
> To many-tower'd Camelot;<br>
> And up and down the people go,<br>
> Gazing where the lilies blow<br>
> Round an island there below,<br>
> The island of Shalott.</p>
> ```

###### 4.8.4.4.9 A group of images that form a single larger picture with no links

When a picture has been sliced into smaller image files that are then displayed together to form the complete picture again, one of the images must have its [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute set as per the relevant rules that would be appropriate for the picture as a whole, and then all the remaining images must have their [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute set to the empty string.

> [!example]
> In the following example, a picture representing a company logo for XYZ Corp has been split into two pieces, the first containing the letters "XYZ" and the second with the word "Corp". The alternative text ("XYZ Corp") is all in the first image.
> 
> ```html
> <h1><img src="logo1.png" alt="XYZ Corp"><img src="logo2.png" alt=""></h1>
> ```

> [!example]
> In the following example, a rating is shown as three filled stars and two empty stars. While the alternative text could have been "★★★☆☆", the author has instead decided to more helpfully give the rating in the form "3 out of 5". That is the alternative text of the first image, and the rest have blank alternative text.
> 
> ```html
> <p>Rating: <meter max=5 value=3><img src="1" alt="3 out of 5"
>   ><img src="1" alt=""><img src="1" alt=""><img src="0" alt=""
>   ><img src="0" alt=""></meter></p>
> ```

###### 4.8.4.4.10 A group of images that form a single larger picture with links

Generally, [image maps](#48141-authoring) should be used instead of slicing an image for links.

However, if an image is indeed sliced and any of the components of the sliced picture are the sole contents of links, then one image per link must have alternative text in its [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute representing the purpose of the link.

> [!example]
> In the following example, a picture representing the flying spaghetti monster emblem, with each of the left noodly appendages and the right noodly appendages in different images, so that the user can pick the left side or the right side in an adventure.
> 
> ```html
> <h1>The Church</h1>
> <p>You come across a flying spaghetti monster. Which side of His
> Noodliness do you wish to reach out for?</p>
> <p><a href="?go=left" ><img src="fsm-left.png"  alt="Left side. "></a
>   ><img src="fsm-middle.png" alt=""
>   ><a href="?go=right"><img src="fsm-right.png" alt="Right side."></a></p>
> ```

###### 4.8.4.4.11 A key part of the content

In some cases, the image is a critical part of the content. This could be the case, for instance, on a page that is part of a photo gallery. The image is the whole *point* of the page containing it.

How to provide alternative text for an image that is a key part of the content depends on the image's provenance.

The general case

When it is possible for detailed alternative text to be provided, for example if the image is part of a series of screenshots in a magazine review, or part of a comic strip, or is a photograph in a blog entry about that photograph, text that can serve as a substitute for the image must be given as the contents of the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute.

> [!example]
> A screenshot in a gallery of screenshots for a new OS, with some alternative text:
> 
> ```html
> <figure>
>  <img src="KDE%20Light%20desktop.png"
>       alt="The desktop is blue, with icons along the left hand side in
>            two columns, reading System, Home, K-Mail, etc. A window is
>            open showing that menus wrap to a second line if they
>            cannot fit in the window. The window has a list of icons
>            along the top, with an address bar below it, a list of
>            icons for tabs along the left edge, a status bar on the
>            bottom, and two panes in the middle. The desktop has a bar
>            at the bottom of the screen with a few buttons, a pager, a
>            list of open applications, and a clock.">
>  <figcaption>Screenshot of a KDE desktop.</figcaption>
> </figure>
> ```

> [!example]
> A graph in a financial report:
> 
> ```html
> <img src="sales.gif"
>      title="Sales graph"
>      alt="From 1998 to 2005, sales increased by the following percentages
>      with each year: 624%, 75%, 138%, 40%, 35%, 9%, 21%">
> ```
> 
> Note that "sales graph" would be inadequate alternative text for a sales graph. Text that would be a good *caption* is not generally suitable as replacement text.

Images that defy a complete description

In certain cases, the nature of the image might be such that providing thorough alternative text is impractical. For example, the image could be indistinct, or could be a complex fractal, or could be a detailed topographical map.

In these cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must contain some suitable alternative text, but it may be somewhat brief.

> [!example]
> Sometimes there simply is no text that can do justice to an image. For example, there is little that can be said to usefully describe a Rorschach inkblot test. However, a description, even if brief, is still better than nothing:
> 
> ```html
> <figure>
>  <img src="/commons/a/a7/Rorschach1.jpg" alt="A shape with left-right
>  symmetry with indistinct edges, with a small gap in the center, two
>  larger gaps offset slightly from the center, with two similar gaps
>  under them. The outline is wider in the top half than the bottom
>  half, with the sides extending upwards higher than the center, and
>  the center extending below the sides.">
>  <figcaption>A black outline of the first of the ten cards
>  in the Rorschach inkblot test.</figcaption>
> </figure>
> ```
> 
> Note that the following would be a very bad use of alternative text:
> 
> ```html
> <!-- This example is wrong. Do not copy it. -->
> <figure>
>  <img src="/commons/a/a7/Rorschach1.jpg" alt="A black outline
>  of the first of the ten cards in the Rorschach inkblot test.">
>  <figcaption>A black outline of the first of the ten cards
>  in the Rorschach inkblot test.</figcaption>
> </figure>
> ```
> 
> Including the caption in the alternative text like this isn't useful because it effectively duplicates the caption for users who don't have images, taunting them twice yet not helping them any more than if they had only read or heard the caption once.

> [!example]
> Another example of an image that defies full description is a fractal, which, by definition, is infinite in detail.
> 
> The following example shows one possible way of providing alternative text for the full view of an image of the Mandelbrot set.
> 
> ```html
> <img src="ms1.jpeg" alt="The Mandelbrot set appears as a cardioid with
> its cusp on the real axis in the positive direction, with a smaller
> bulb aligned along the same center line, touching it in the negative
> direction, and with these two shapes being surrounded by smaller bulbs
> of various sizes.">
> ```

> [!example]
> Similarly, a photograph of a person's face, for example in a biography, can be considered quite relevant and key to the content, but it can be hard to fully substitute text for:
> 
> ```html
> <section class="bio">
>  <h1>A Biography of Isaac Asimov</h1>
>  <p>Born <b>Isaak Yudovich Ozimov</b> in 1920, Isaac was a prolific author.</p>
>  <p><img src="headpics/asimov.jpeg" alt="Isaac Asimov had dark hair, a tall forehead, and wore glasses.
>  Later in life, he wore long white sideburns."></p>
>  <p>Asimov was born in Russia, and moved to the US when he was three years old.</p>
>  <p>...</p>
> </section>
> ```
> 
> In such cases it is unnecessary (and indeed discouraged) to include a reference to the presence of the image itself in the alternative text, since such text would be redundant with the browser itself reporting the presence of the image. For example, if the alternative text was "A photo of Isaac Asimov", then a conforming user agent might read that out as "(Image) A photo of Isaac Asimov" rather than the more useful "(Image) Isaac Asimov had dark hair, a tall forehead, and wore glasses...".

Images whose contents are not known

In some unfortunate cases, there might be no alternative text available at all, either because the image is obtained in some automated fashion without any associated alternative text (e.g., a webcam), or because the page is being generated by a script using user-provided images where the user did not provide suitable or usable alternative text (e.g. photograph sharing sites), or because the author does not themself know what the images represent (e.g. a blind photographer sharing an image on their blog).

In such cases, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute may be omitted, but one of the following conditions must be met as well:
- The [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element is in a [`figure`](#4412-the-figure-element) element that contains a [`figcaption`](#4413-the-figcaption-element) element that contains content other than [inter-element whitespace](#325-content-models), and, ignoring the [`figcaption`](#4413-the-figcaption-element) element and its descendants, the [`figure`](#4412-the-figure-element) element has no [flow content](#32522-flow-content) descendants other than [inter-element whitespace](#325-content-models) and the [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element.
- The [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute is present and has a non-empty value.

  > [!note]
  > Relying on the [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute is currently discouraged as many user agents do not expose the attribute in an accessible manner as required by this specification (e.g. requiring a pointing device such as a mouse to cause a tooltip to appear, which excludes keyboard-only users and touch-only users, such as anyone with a modern phone or tablet).

> [!note]
> Such cases are to be kept to an absolute minimum. If there is even the slightest possibility of the author having the ability to provide real alternative text, then it would not be acceptable to omit the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute.

> [!example]
> A photo on a photo-sharing site, if the site received the image with no metadata other than the caption, could be marked up as follows:
> 
> ```html
> <figure>
>  <img src="1100670787_6a7c664aef.jpg">
>  <figcaption>Bubbles traveled everywhere with us.</figcaption>
> </figure>
> ```
> 
> It would be better, however, if a detailed description of the important parts of the image obtained from the user and included on the page.

> [!example]
> A blind user's blog in which a photo taken by the user is shown. Initially, the user might not have any idea what the photo they took shows:
> 
> ```html
> <article>
>  <h1>I took a photo</h1>
>  <p>I went out today and took a photo!</p>
>  <figure>
>   <img src="photo2.jpeg">
>   <figcaption>A photograph taken blindly from my front porch.</figcaption>
>  </figure>
> </article>
> ```
> 
> Eventually though, the user might obtain a description of the image from their friends and could then include alternative text:
> 
> ```html
> <article>
>  <h1>I took a photo</h1>
>  <p>I went out today and took a photo!</p>
>  <figure>
>   <img src="photo2.jpeg" alt="The photograph shows my squirrel
>   feeder hanging from the edge of my roof. It is half full, but there
>   are no squirrels around. In the background, out-of-focus trees fill the
>   shot. The feeder is made of wood with a metal grate, and it contains
>   peanuts. The edge of the roof is wooden too, and is painted white
>   with light blue streaks.">
>   <figcaption>A photograph taken blindly from my front porch.</figcaption>
>  </figure>
> </article>
> ```

> [!example]
> Sometimes the entire point of the image is that a textual description is not available, and the user is to provide the description. For instance, the point of a CAPTCHA image is to see if the user can literally read the graphic. Here is one way to mark up a CAPTCHA (note the [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute):
> 
> ```html
> <p><label>What does this image say?
> <img src="captcha.cgi?id=8934" title="CAPTCHA">
> <input type=text name=captcha></label>
> (If you cannot see the image, you can use an <a
> href="?audio">audio</a> test instead.)</p>
> ```
> 
> Another example would be software that displays images and asks for alternative text precisely for the purpose of then writing a page with correct alternative text. Such a page could have a table of images, like this:
> 
> ```html
> <table>
>  <thead>
>   <tr> <th> Image <th> Description
>  <tbody>
>   <tr>
>    <td> <img src="2421.png" title="Image 640 by 100, filename 'banner.gif'">
>    <td> <input name="alt2421">
>   <tr>
>    <td> <img src="2422.png" title="Image 200 by 480, filename 'ad3.gif'">
>    <td> <input name="alt2422">
> </table>
> ```
> 
> Notice that even in this example, as much useful information as possible is still included in the [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute.

> [!note]
> Since some users cannot use images at all (e.g. because they have a very slow connection, or because they are using a text-only browser, or because they are listening to the page being read out by a hands-free automobile voice web browser, or simply because they are blind), the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute is only allowed to be omitted rather than being provided with replacement text when no alternative text is available and none can be made available, as in the above examples. Lack of effort from the part of the author is not an acceptable reason for omitting the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute.

###### 4.8.4.4.12 An image not intended for the user

Generally authors should avoid using [`img`](#483-the-img-element) elements for purposes other than showing images.

If an [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element is being used for purposes other than showing an image, e.g. as part of a service to count page views, then the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute must be the empty string.

In such cases, the [`width`](#4817-dimension-attributes) and [`height`](#4817-dimension-attributes) attributes should both be set to zero.

###### 4.8.4.4.13 An image in an email or private document intended for a specific person who is known to be able to view images

*This section does not apply to documents that are publicly accessible, or whose target audience is not necessarily personally known to the author, such as documents on a web site, emails sent to public mailing lists, or software documentation.*

When an image is included in a private communication (such as an HTML email) aimed at a specific person who is known to be able to view images, the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute may be omitted. However, even in such cases authors are strongly urged to include alternative text (as appropriate according to the kind of image involved, as described in the above entries), so that the email is still usable should the user use a mail client that does not support images, or should the document be forwarded on to other users whose abilities might not include easily seeing images.

###### 4.8.4.4.14 Guidance for markup generators

Markup generators (such as WYSIWYG authoring tools) should, wherever possible, obtain alternative text from their users. However, it is recognized that in many cases, this will not be possible.

For images that are the sole contents of links, markup generators should examine the link target to determine the title of the target, or the URL of the target, and use information obtained in this manner as the alternative text.

For images that have captions, markup generators should use the [`figure`](#4412-the-figure-element) and [`figcaption`](#4413-the-figcaption-element) elements, or the [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute, to provide the image's caption.

As a last resort, implementers should either set the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute to the empty string, under the assumption that the image is a purely decorative image that doesn't add any information but is still specific to the surrounding content, or omit the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute altogether, under the assumption that the image is a key part of the content.

Markup generators may specify a `generator-unable-to-provide-required-alt` attribute on [`img`](#483-the-img-element) elements for which they have been unable to obtain alternative text and for which they have therefore omitted the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute. The value of this attribute must be the empty string. Documents containing such attributes are not conforming, but conformance checkers will [silently ignore](#484415-guidance-for-conformance-checkers) this error.

> [!note]
> This is intended to avoid markup generators from being pressured into replacing the error of omitting the [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute with the even more egregious error of providing phony alternative text, because state-of-the-art automated conformance checkers cannot distinguish phony alternative text from correct alternative text.

Markup generators should generally avoid using the image's own filename as the alternative text. Similarly, markup generators should avoid generating alternative text from any content that will be equally available to presentation user agents (e.g., web browsers).

> [!note]
> This is because once a page is generated, it will typically not be updated, whereas the browsers that later read the page can be updated by the user, therefore the browser is likely to have more up-to-date and finely-tuned heuristics than the markup generator did when generating the page.

###### 4.8.4.4.15 Guidance for conformance checkers

A conformance checker must report the lack of an [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute as an error unless one of the conditions listed below applies:
- The [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element is in a [`figure`](#4412-the-figure-element) element that satisfies [the conditions described above](#484411-a-key-part-of-the-content).
- The [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element has a [`title`](#3261-the-title-attribute) attribute with a value that is not the empty string (also as [described above](#484411-a-key-part-of-the-content)).
- The conformance checker has been configured to assume that the document is an email or document intended for a specific person who is known to be able to view images.
- The [`img`](#483-the-img-element) element has a (non-conforming) [`generator-unable-to-provide-required-alt`](#484414-guidance-for-markup-generators) attribute whose value is the empty string. A conformance checker that is not reporting the lack of an [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute as an error must also not report the presence of the empty [`generator-unable-to-provide-required-alt`](#484414-guidance-for-markup-generators) attribute as an error. (This case does not represent a case where the document is conforming, only that the generator could not determine appropriate alternative text — validators are not required to show an error in this case, because such an error might encourage markup generators to include bogus alternative text purely in an attempt to silence validators. Naturally, conformance checkers *may* report the lack of an [`alt`](#483-the-img-element) attribute as an error even in the presence of the [`generator-unable-to-provide-required-alt`](#484414-guidance-for-markup-generators) attribute; for example, there could be a user option to report *all* conformance errors even those that might be the more or less inevitable result of using a markup generator.)

#### 4.8.5 The `iframe` element

[Categories](#324-element-definitions):

[Flow content](#32522-flow-content).

[Phrasing content](#32525-phrasing-content).

[Embedded content](#32526-embedded-content).

[Interactive content](#32527-interactive-content).

[Palpable content](#32528-palpable-content).

[Contexts in which this element can be used](#324-element-definitions):

Where [embedded content](#32526-embedded-content) is expected.

[Content model](#324-element-definitions):

[Nothing](#3251-the-nothing-content-model).

[Tag omission in text/html](#324-element-definitions):

Neither tag is omissible.

[Content attributes](#324-element-definitions):

[Global attributes](#326-global-attributes)

[`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) — Address of the resource

[`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) — A document to render in the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)

[`name`](#485-the-iframe-element) — Name of [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)

[`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) — Security rules for nested content

[`allow`](#485-the-iframe-element) — [Permissions policy](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-feature-policy/#permissions-policy) to be applied to the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s contents

[`allowfullscreen`](#485-the-iframe-element) — Whether to allow the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s contents to use [`requestFullscreen()`](https://fullscreen.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-element-requestfullscreen)

[`width`](#4817-dimension-attributes) — Horizontal dimension

[`height`](#4817-dimension-attributes) — Vertical dimension

[`referrerpolicy`](#485-the-iframe-element) — [Referrer policy](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-referrer-policy/#referrer-policy) for [fetches](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-fetch) initiated by the element

[`loading`](#485-the-iframe-element) — Used when determining loading deferral

[Accessibility considerations](#324-element-definitions):

[For authors](https://w3c.github.io/html-aria/#el-iframe).

[For implementers](https://w3c.github.io/html-aam/#el-iframe).

[Sanitization](#324-element-definitions):

[Unsafe](#865-sanitization-constants).

[DOM interface](#324-element-definitions):

```webidl
[Exposed=Window]
interface HTMLIFrameElement : HTMLElement {
  [HTMLConstructor] constructor();

  [CEReactions, ReflectURL] attribute USVString src;
  [CEReactions] attribute (TrustedHTML or DOMString) srcdoc;
  [CEReactions, Reflect] attribute DOMString name;
  [SameObject, PutForwards=value, Reflect] readonly attribute DOMTokenList sandbox;
  [CEReactions, Reflect] attribute DOMString allow;
  [CEReactions, Reflect] attribute boolean allowFullscreen;
  [CEReactions, Reflect] attribute DOMString width;
  [CEReactions, Reflect] attribute DOMString height;
  [CEReactions] attribute DOMString referrerPolicy;
  [CEReactions] attribute DOMString loading;
  readonly attribute Document? contentDocument;
  readonly attribute WindowProxy? contentWindow;
  Document? getSVGDocument();

  // also has obsolete members
};
```

The [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element [represents](#322-elements-in-the-dom) its [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables).

The `src` attribute gives the [URL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url) of a page that the element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) is to contain. The attribute, if present, must be a [valid non-empty URL potentially surrounded by spaces](#241-terminology). If the [`itemprop`](#523-names-the-itemprop-attribute) attribute is specified on an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element, then the [`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute must also be specified.

The `srcdoc` attribute gives the content of the page that the element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) is to contain. The value of the attribute is used to [construct](#745-populating-a-session-history-entry) an `iframe` `srcdoc` document, which is a [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) whose [URL](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#45-interface-document) [matches `about:srcdoc`](#241-terminology).

The [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute, if present, must have a value using [the HTML syntax](#13-the-html-syntax) that consists of the following syntactic components, in the given order:
1. Any number of [comments](#1316-comments) and [ASCII whitespace](infra-spec-whatwg-org.md#46-code-points).
2. Optionally, a [DOCTYPE](#1311-the-doctype).
3. Any number of [comments](#1316-comments) and [ASCII whitespace](infra-spec-whatwg-org.md#46-code-points).
4. The [document element](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#421-document-tree), in the form of an [`html`](#411-the-html-element) [element](#1312-elements).
5. Any number of [comments](#1316-comments) and [ASCII whitespace](infra-spec-whatwg-org.md#46-code-points).

> [!note]
> The above requirements apply in [XML documents](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#45-interface-document) as well.

> [!example]
> Here a blog uses the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute in conjunction with the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute described below to provide users of user agents that support this feature with an extra layer of protection from script injection in the blog post comments:
> 
> ```html
> <article>
>  <h1>I got my own magazine!</h1>
>  <p>After much effort, I've finally found a publisher, and so now I
>  have my own magazine! Isn't that awesome?! The first issue will come
>  out in September, and we have articles about getting food, and about
>  getting in boxes, it's going to be great!</p>
>  <footer>
>   <p>Written by <a href="/users/cap">cap</a>, 1 hour ago.
>  </footer>
>  <article>
>   <footer> Thirteen minutes ago, <a href="/users/ch">ch</a> wrote: </footer>
>   <iframe sandbox srcdoc="<p>did you get a cover picture yet?"></iframe>
>  </article>
>  <article>
>   <footer> Nine minutes ago, <a href="/users/cap">cap</a> wrote: </footer>
>   <iframe sandbox srcdoc="<p>Yeah, you can see it <a href=&quot;/gallery?mode=cover&amp;amp;page=1&quot;>in my gallery</a>."></iframe>
>  </article>
>  <article>
>   <footer> Five minutes ago, <a href="/users/ch">ch</a> wrote: </footer>
>   <iframe sandbox srcdoc="<p>hey that's earl's table.
> <p>you should get earl&amp;amp;me on the next cover."></iframe>
>  </article>
> ```
> 
> Notice the way that quotes have to be escaped (otherwise the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute would end prematurely), and the way raw ampersands (e.g. in URLs or in prose) mentioned in the sandboxed content have to be *doubly* escaped — once so that the ampersand is preserved when originally parsing the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute, and once more to prevent the ampersand from being misinterpreted when parsing the sandboxed content.
> 
> Furthermore, notice that since the [DOCTYPE](#1311-the-doctype) is optional in [`iframe` `srcdoc` documents](#485-the-iframe-element), and the [`html`](#411-the-html-element), [`head`](#421-the-head-element), and [`body`](#431-the-body-element) elements have [optional start and end tags](#13124-optional-tags), and the [`title`](#422-the-title-element) element is also optional in [`iframe` `srcdoc` documents](#485-the-iframe-element), the markup in a [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute can be relatively succinct despite representing an entire document, since only the contents of the [`body`](#431-the-body-element) element need appear literally in the syntax. The other elements are still present, but only by implication.

> [!note]
> In [the HTML syntax](#13-the-html-syntax), authors need only remember to use U+0022 QUOTATION MARK characters (") to wrap the attribute contents and then to escape all U+0026 AMPERSAND (&) and U+0022 QUOTATION MARK (") characters, and to specify the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute, to ensure safe embedding of content. (And remember to escape ampersands before quotation marks, to ensure quotation marks become &quot; and not &amp;quot;.)

> [!note]
> In XML the U+003C LESS-THAN SIGN character (<) needs to be escaped as well. In order to prevent [attribute-value normalization](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#AVNormalize), some of XML's whitespace characters — specifically U+0009 CHARACTER TABULATION (tab), U+000A LINE FEED (LF), and U+000D CARRIAGE RETURN (CR) — also need to be escaped. [\[XML\]](#references)

> [!note]
> If the [`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute and the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute are both specified together, the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute takes priority. This allows authors to provide a fallback [URL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url) for legacy user agents that do not support the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute.

---

The [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) [HTML element post-connection steps](#214-dom-trees), given insertedNode, are:
1. If insertedNode's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node)'s [browsing context](#732-browsing-contexts) is null, then return.
2. If insertedNode has a [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute, then [parse the sandboxing directive](#715-sandboxing) given the attribute's value and insertedNode's [`iframe` sandboxing flag set](#715-sandboxing).
3. [Create a new child navigable](#7313-child-navigables) for insertedNode.
4. [Process the `iframe` attributes](#485-the-iframe-element) for insertedNode, with *[initialInsertion](#485-the-iframe-element)* set to true.

The [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) [HTML element removing steps](#214-dom-trees), given removedNode, are to [destroy a child navigable](#7316-navigable-destruction) given removedNode.

> [!note]
> This happens without any [`unload`](#events) events firing (the element's [content document](#7313-child-navigables) is *[destroyed](#7316-navigable-destruction)*, not *[unloaded](#759-unloading-documents)*).

> [!warning]
> Although [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)s are processed while in a [shadow tree](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#422-shadow-tree), per the above, several other aspects of their behavior are not well-defined with regards to shadow trees. See [issue #763](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/763) for more detail.

Whenever an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element with a non-null [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) has its [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute set, changed, or removed, the user agent must [process the `iframe` attributes](#485-the-iframe-element).

Similarly, whenever an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element with a non-null [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) but with no [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute specified has its [`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute set, changed, or removed, the user agent must [process the `iframe` attributes](#485-the-iframe-element).

To process the `iframe` attributes for an element element, with an optional boolean initialInsertion (default false):
1. If element's [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is specified:
   1. Set element's [current navigation was lazy loaded](#485-the-iframe-element) boolean to false.
   2. If the [will lazy load element steps](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) given element return true:
      1. Set element's [lazy load resumption steps](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) to the rest of this algorithm starting with the step labeled *navigate to the srcdoc resource*.
      2. Set element's [current navigation was lazy loaded](#485-the-iframe-element) boolean to true.
      3. [Start intersection-observing a lazy loading element](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) for element.
      4. Return.
   3. *Navigate to the srcdoc resource*: [Navigate an `iframe` or `frame`](#485-the-iframe-element) given element, [`about:srcdoc`](#241-terminology), the empty string, and the value of element's [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute.

      The resulting [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) must be considered [an `iframe` `srcdoc` document](#485-the-iframe-element).

2. Otherwise:
   1. Let url be the result of running the [shared attribute processing steps for `iframe` and `frame` elements](#485-the-iframe-element) given element and initialInsertion.
   2. If url is null, then return.
   3. If url [matches `about:blank`](#241-terminology) and initialInsertion is true:
      1. Run the [iframe load event steps](#485-the-iframe-element) given element.
      2. Return.
   4. Let referrerPolicy be the current state of element's [`referrerpolicy`](#485-the-iframe-element) content attribute.
   5. Set element's [current navigation was lazy loaded](#485-the-iframe-element) boolean to false.
   6. If the [will lazy load element steps](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) given element return true:
      1. Set element's [lazy load resumption steps](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) to the rest of this algorithm starting with the step labeled *navigate*.
      2. Set element's [current navigation was lazy loaded](#485-the-iframe-element) boolean to true.
      3. [Start intersection-observing a lazy loading element](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) for element.
      4. Return.
   7. *Navigate*: [Navigate an `iframe` or `frame`](#485-the-iframe-element) given element, url, referrerPolicy, null, and initialInsertion.

The shared attribute processing steps for `iframe` and `frame` elements, given an element element and a boolean initialInsertion, are:
1. Let url be the [URL record](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url) [`about:blank`](#219-dependencies).
2. If element has a [`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute specified, and its value is not the empty string:
   1. Let maybeURL be the result of [encoding-parsing a URL](#242-parsing-urls) given that attribute's value, relative to element's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node).
   2. If maybeURL is not failure, then set url to maybeURL.
3. If the [inclusive ancestor navigables](#7315-related-navigable-collections) of element's [node navigable](#731-navigables) contains a [navigable](#731-navigables) whose [active document](#731-navigables)'s [URL](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#45-interface-document) [equals](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url-equals) url with *[exclude fragments](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#url-equals-exclude-fragments)* set to true, then return null.
4. If url [matches `about:blank`](#241-terminology) and initialInsertion is true, then perform the [URL and history update steps](#744-non-fragment-synchronous-navigations) given element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active document](#731-navigables) and url.

   > [!note]
   > This is necessary in case url is something like `about:blank?foo`. If url is just plain `about:blank`, this will do nothing.

5. Return url.

To navigate an `iframe` or `frame` given an element element, a [URL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url) url, a [referrer policy](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-referrer-policy/#referrer-policy) referrerPolicy, an optional string-or-null srcdocString (default null), and an optional boolean initialInsertion (default false):
1. Let historyHandling be "[`auto`](#7421-supporting-concepts)".
2. If element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active document](#731-navigables) is not [completely loaded](#758-finishing-the-loading-process), then set historyHandling to "[`replace`](#7421-supporting-concepts)".
3. If element is an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element):
   1. Set element's [pending resource-timing start time](#485-the-iframe-element) to the [current high resolution time](https://w3c.github.io/hr-time/#dfn-current-high-resolution-time) given element's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node)'s [relevant global object](#81334-relevant).
   2. Set element's [pending resource-timing URL](#485-the-iframe-element) to url.
4. [Navigate](#7422-beginning-navigation) element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) to url using element's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node), with *[historyHandling](#7422-beginning-navigation)* set to historyHandling, *[referrerPolicy](#7422-beginning-navigation)* set to referrerPolicy, *[documentResource](#7422-beginning-navigation)* set to srcdocString, and *[initialInsertion](#7422-beginning-navigation)* set to initialInsertion.

Each [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) has an iframe load in progress flag and a mute iframe load flag. When a [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) is created, these flags must be unset for that [`Document`](#311-the-document-object).

To run the iframe load event steps, given an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element element:
1. [Assert](infra-spec-whatwg-org.md#310-assertions): element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) is not null.
2. Let childDocument be element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active document](#731-navigables).
3. If childDocument has its [mute iframe load](#485-the-iframe-element) flag set, then return.
4. If element's [pending resource-timing start time](#485-the-iframe-element) is not null:
   1. [Assert](infra-spec-whatwg-org.md#310-assertions): element's [pending resource-timing URL](#485-the-iframe-element) is not null.
   2. Let global be element's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node)'s [relevant global object](#81334-relevant).
   3. Let fallbackTimingInfo be a new [fetch timing info](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-timing-info) whose [start time](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-timing-info-start-time) is element's [pending resource-timing start time](#485-the-iframe-element) and whose [response end time](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-timing-info-end-time) is the [current high resolution time](https://w3c.github.io/hr-time/#dfn-current-high-resolution-time) given global.
   4. [Mark resource timing](https://w3c.github.io/resource-timing/#dfn-mark-resource-timing) given fallbackTimingInfo, the result of [parsing](#242-parsing-urls) element's [pending resource-timing URL](#485-the-iframe-element), "[`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)", global, the empty string, a new [response body info](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#response-body-info), and 0.
   5. Set element's [pending resource-timing start time](#485-the-iframe-element) to null.
   6. Set element's [pending resource-timing URL](#485-the-iframe-element) to null.
5. Set childDocument's [iframe load in progress](#485-the-iframe-element) flag.
6. [Fire an event](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#210-firing-events) named [`load`](#events) at element.
7. Unset childDocument's [iframe load in progress](#485-the-iframe-element) flag.

> [!warning]
> This, in conjunction with scripting, can be used to probe the URL space of the local network's HTTP servers. User agents may implement [cross-origin](#711-origins) access control policies that are stricter than those described above to mitigate this attack, but unfortunately such policies are typically not compatible with existing web content.

If an element type potentially delays the load event, then for each element element of that type, the user agent must [delay the load event](#1327-the-end) of element's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node) if element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) is non-null and any of the following are true:
- element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active document](#731-navigables) is not [ready for post-load tasks](#1327-the-end);
- element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [is delaying `load` events](#731-navigables) is true; or
- anything is [delaying the load event](#1327-the-end) of element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active document](#731-navigables).

> [!note]
> If, during the handling of the [`load`](#events) event, element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) is again [navigated](#7422-beginning-navigation), that will further [delay the load event](#1327-the-end).

Each [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element has an associated current navigation was lazy loaded boolean, initially false. It is set and unset in the [process the `iframe` attributes](#485-the-iframe-element) algorithm.

An [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element whose [current navigation was lazy loaded](#485-the-iframe-element) boolean is false [potentially delays the load event](#485-the-iframe-element).

Each [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element has an associated null or [`DOMHighResTimeStamp`](https://w3c.github.io/hr-time/#dom-domhighrestimestamp) pending resource-timing start time, initially set to null.

Each [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element has an associated null or [URL](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-url) pending resource-timing URL, initially set to null.

> [!note]
> If, when the element is created, the [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is not set, and the [`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is either also not set or set but its value cannot be [parsed](#242-parsing-urls), the element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) will remain at the [initial `about:blank`](#311-the-document-object) [`Document`](#311-the-document-object).

> [!note]
> If the user [navigates](#7422-beginning-navigation) away from this page, the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active `WindowProxy`](#731-navigables) object will proxy new [`Window`](#722-the-window-object) objects for new [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) objects, but the [`src`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute will not change.

---

The `name` attribute, if present, must be a [valid navigable target name](#7317-navigable-target-names). The given value is used to name the element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) if present when that is [created](#7313-child-navigables).

---

The `sandbox` attribute, when specified, enables a set of extra restrictions on any content hosted by the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element). Its value must be an [unordered set of unique space-separated tokens](#237-space-separated-tokens) that are [ASCII case-insensitive](infra-spec-whatwg-org.md#47-strings). The allowed values are:
- [`allow-downloads`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-forms`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-modals`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-orientation-lock`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-pointer-lock`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-popups`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-presentation`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-same-origin`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-scripts`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-top-navigation`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation`](#715-sandboxing)
- [`allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocols`](#715-sandboxing)

When the attribute is set, the content is treated as being from a unique [opaque origin](#711-origins), forms, scripts, and various potentially annoying APIs are disabled, and links are prevented from targeting other [navigables](#731-navigables). The [`allow-same-origin`](#715-sandboxing) keyword causes the content to be treated as being from its real origin instead of forcing it into an [opaque origin](#711-origins); the [`allow-top-navigation`](#715-sandboxing) keyword allows the content to [navigate](#7422-beginning-navigation) its [traversable navigable](#7311-traversable-navigables); the [`allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation`](#715-sandboxing) keyword behaves similarly but allows such [navigation](#7422-beginning-navigation) only when the browsing context's [active window](#731-navigables) has [transient activation](#641-data-model); the [`allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocols`](#715-sandboxing) reenables navigations toward non [fetch scheme](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-scheme) to be [handed off to external software](#74234-non-fetch-schemes-and-external-software); and the [`allow-forms`](#715-sandboxing), [`allow-modals`](#715-sandboxing), [`allow-orientation-lock`](#715-sandboxing), [`allow-pointer-lock`](#715-sandboxing), [`allow-popups`](#715-sandboxing), [`allow-presentation`](#715-sandboxing), [`allow-scripts`](#715-sandboxing), and [`allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox`](#715-sandboxing) keywords re-enable forms, modal dialogs, screen orientation lock, the pointer lock API, popups, the presentation API, scripts, and the creation of unsandboxed [auxiliary browsing contexts](#732-browsing-contexts) respectively. The [`allow-downloads`](#715-sandboxing) keyword allows content to perform downloads. [\[POINTERLOCK\]](#references) [\[SCREENORIENTATION\]](#references) [\[PRESENTATION\]](#references)

The [`allow-top-navigation`](#715-sandboxing) and [`allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation`](#715-sandboxing) keywords must not both be specified, as doing so is redundant; only [`allow-top-navigation`](#715-sandboxing) will have an effect in such non-conformant markup.

Similarly, the [`allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocols`](#715-sandboxing) keyword must not be specified if either [`allow-top-navigation`](#715-sandboxing) or [`allow-popups`](#715-sandboxing) are specified, as doing so is redundant.

> [!warning]
> Setting both the [`allow-scripts`](#715-sandboxing) and [`allow-same-origin`](#715-sandboxing) keywords together when the embedded page has the [same origin](#711-origins) as the page containing the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) allows the embedded page to simply remove the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute and then reload itself, effectively breaking out of the sandbox altogether.

> [!warning]
> These flags only take effect when the [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) of the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element is [navigated](#7422-beginning-navigation). Removing them, or removing the entire [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute, has no effect on an already-loaded page.

> [!warning]
> Potentially hostile files should not be served from the same server as the file containing the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element. Sandboxing hostile content is of minimal help if an attacker can convince the user to just visit the hostile content directly, rather than in the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element). To limit the damage that can be caused by hostile HTML content, it should be served from a separate dedicated domain. Using a different domain ensures that scripts in the files are unable to attack the site, even if the user is tricked into visiting those pages directly, without the protection of the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute.

When an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is set or changed while it has a non-null [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables), the user agent must [parse the sandboxing directive](#715-sandboxing) given the attribute's value and the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [`iframe` sandboxing flag set](#715-sandboxing).

When an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is removed while it has a non-null [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables), the user agent must empty the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [`iframe` sandboxing flag set](#715-sandboxing).

> [!example]
> In this example, some completely-unknown, potentially hostile, user-provided HTML content is embedded in a page. Because it is served from a separate domain, it is affected by all the normal cross-site restrictions. In addition, the embedded page has scripting disabled, plugins disabled, forms disabled, and it cannot navigate any frames or windows other than itself (or any frames or windows it itself embeds).
> 
> ```html
> <p>We're not scared of you! Here is your content, unedited:</p>
> <iframe sandbox src="https://usercontent.example.net/getusercontent.cgi?id=12193"></iframe>
> ```
> 
> > [!warning]
> > It is important to use a separate domain so that if the attacker convinces the user to visit that page directly, the page doesn't run in the context of the site's origin, which would make the user vulnerable to any attack found in the page.

> [!example]
> In this example, a gadget from another site is embedded. The gadget has scripting and forms enabled, and the origin sandbox restrictions are lifted, allowing the gadget to communicate with its originating server. The sandbox is still useful, however, as it disables plugins and popups, thus reducing the risk of the user being exposed to malware and other annoyances.
> 
> ```html
> <iframe sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-scripts"
>         src="https://maps.example.com/embedded.html"></iframe>
> ```

> [!example]
> Suppose a file A contained the following fragment:
> 
> ```html
> <iframe sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-forms" src=B></iframe>
> ```
> 
> Suppose that file B contained an iframe also:
> 
> ```html
> <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" src=C></iframe>
> ```
> 
> Further, suppose that file C contained a link:
> 
> ```html
> <a href=D>Link</a>
> ```
> 
> For this example, suppose all the files were served as [`text/html`](#171-texthtml).
> 
> Page C in this scenario has all the sandboxing flags set. Scripts are disabled, because the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) in A has scripts disabled, and this overrides the [`allow-scripts`](#715-sandboxing) keyword set on the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) in B. Forms are also disabled, because the inner [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) (in B) does not have the [`allow-forms`](#715-sandboxing) keyword set.
> 
> Suppose now that a script in A removes all the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attributes in A and B. This would change nothing immediately. If the user clicked the link in C, loading page D into the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) in B, page D would now act as if the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) in B had the [`allow-same-origin`](#715-sandboxing) and [`allow-forms`](#715-sandboxing) keywords set, because that was the state of the [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) in the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) in A when page B was loaded.
> 
> Generally speaking, dynamically removing or changing the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is ill-advised, because it can make it quite hard to reason about what will be allowed and what will not.

---

The `allow` attribute, when specified, determines the [container policy](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-feature-policy/#container-policy) that will be used when the [permissions policy](#311-the-document-object) for a [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) in the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) is initialized. Its value must be a [serialized permissions policy](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-feature-policy/#serialized-permissions-policy). [\[PERMISSIONSPOLICY\]](#references)

> [!example]
> In this example, an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) is used to embed a map from an online navigation service. The [`allow`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is used to enable the Geolocation API within the nested context.
> 
> ```html
> <iframe src="https://maps.example.com/" allow="geolocation"></iframe>
> ```

The `allowfullscreen` attribute is a [boolean attribute](#232-boolean-attributes). When specified, it indicates that [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) objects in the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) will be initialized with a [permissions policy](#311-the-document-object) which allows the "`fullscreen`" feature to be used from any [origin](#711-origins). This is enforced by the [process permissions policy attributes](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-feature-policy/#process-policy-attributes) algorithm. [\[PERMISSIONSPOLICY\]](#references)

> [!example]
> Here, an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) is used to embed a player from a video site. The [`allowfullscreen`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute is needed to enable the player to show its video fullscreen.
> 
> ```html
> <article>
>  <header>
>   <p><img src="/usericons/1627591962735"> <b>Fred Flintstone</b></p>
>   <p><a href="/posts/3095182851" rel=bookmark>12:44</a> — <a href="#acl-3095182851">Private Post</a></p>
>  </header>
>  <p>Check out my new ride!</p>
>  <iframe src="https://video.example.com/embed?id=92469812" allowfullscreen></iframe>
> </article>
> ```

> [!note]
> Neither [`allow`](#485-the-iframe-element) nor [`allowfullscreen`](#485-the-iframe-element) can grant access to a feature in an [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) if the element's [node document](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#44-interface-node) is not already allowed to use that feature.

To determine whether a [`Document`](#311-the-document-object) object document is allowed to use the policy-controlled-feature feature, run these steps:
1. If document's [browsing context](#732-browsing-contexts) is null, then return false.
2. If document is not [fully active](#733-fully-active-documents), then return false.
3. If the result of running [is feature enabled in document for origin](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-feature-policy/#is-feature-enabled) on feature, document, and document's [origin](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#45-interface-document) is "`Enabled`", then return true.
4. Return false.

> [!warning]
> Because they only influence the [permissions policy](#311-the-document-object) of the [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables)'s [active document](#731-navigables), the [`allow`](#485-the-iframe-element) and [`allowfullscreen`](#485-the-iframe-element) attributes only take effect when the [content navigable](#7313-child-navigables) of the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) is [navigated](#7422-beginning-navigation). Adding or removing them has no effect on an already-loaded document.

---

The [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element supports [dimension attributes](#4817-dimension-attributes) for cases where the embedded content has specific dimensions (e.g. ad units have well-defined dimensions).

An [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element never has [fallback content](#32526-embedded-content), as it will always [create a new child navigable](#7313-child-navigables), regardless of whether the specified initial contents are successfully used.

---

The `referrerpolicy` attribute is a [referrer policy attribute](#255-referrer-policy-attributes). Its purpose is to set the [referrer policy](https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-referrer-policy/#referrer-policy) used when [processing the `iframe` attributes](#485-the-iframe-element) as well as allowing masking of some [origins](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#45-interface-document) in the [internal ancestor origin objects list creation steps](#313-ancestor-origins). [\[REFERRERPOLICY\]](#references)

The `loading` attribute is a [lazy loading attribute](#257-lazy-loading-attributes). Its purpose is to indicate the policy for loading [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) elements that are outside the viewport.

When the [`loading`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute's state is changed to the [Eager](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) state, the user agent must run these steps:
1. Let resumptionSteps be the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) element's [lazy load resumption steps](#257-lazy-loading-attributes).
2. If resumptionSteps is null, then return.
3. Set the [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s [lazy load resumption steps](#257-lazy-loading-attributes) to null.
4. Invoke resumptionSteps.

---

Descendants of [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) elements represent nothing. (In legacy user agents that do not support [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) elements, the contents would be parsed as markup that could act as fallback content.)

> [!note]
> The [HTML parser](#132-parsing-html-documents) treats markup inside [`iframe`](#485-the-iframe-element) elements as text.

---

The `srcdoc` getter steps are:
1. Let attribute be the result of [getting an attribute by namespace and local name](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#49-interface-element) given null, [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s [local name](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#492-interface-attr), and [this](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#this).
2. If attribute is null, then return the empty string.
3. Return attribute's [value](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#492-interface-attr).

The [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element) setter steps are:
1. Let compliantString be the result of invoking the [get trusted type compliant string](https://w3c.github.io/trusted-types/dist/spec/#get-trusted-type-compliant-string) algorithm with [`TrustedHTML`](https://w3c.github.io/trusted-types/dist/spec/#trustedhtml), [this](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#this)'s [relevant global object](#81334-relevant), the given value, "`HTMLIFrameElement srcdoc`", and "`script`".
2. [Set an attribute value](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#49-interface-element) given [this](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#this), [`srcdoc`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s [local name](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#492-interface-attr), and compliantString.

The [supported tokens](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#71-interface-domtokenlist) for [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element)'s [`DOMTokenList`](dom-spec-whatwg-org.md#71-interface-domtokenlist) are the allowed values defined in the [`sandbox`](#485-the-iframe-element) attribute and supported by the user agent.
